526.title: Sita won't stay behind
526.hook: Rama asks Sita to wait at home, and she claims her share of his road
526.carry: a partner in dharma shares the road
526.tomorrow: Rama has a list of dangers. will it stop her?
526.howItsDone: At a Hindu wedding the couple takes seven steps together beside the sacred fire (saptapadi) and become partners in dharma; Sita's argument can be read as what that promise means when the road turns hard.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's calm toward blame. This is daiva, he said: daiva: larger than anyone's fault. A new week begins, and Sita speaks.

Rama comes home with his news, and with a plan for Sita. She'll stay in Ayodhya and wait for him. He has thought it through, kindly, carefully, and alone. In Valmiki's telling, Sita is many things in this scene, and quiet isn't the first of them. She hears the whole plan out. Then, piece by piece, she takes it apart.
screen: `RAMA'S PLAN FOR SITA.` → `KINDLY, CAREFULLY, ALONE.` → `SHE TAKES THE PLAN APART.`

segments.voice: Sita has been waiting at home for the procession. She sees Rama come in alone and pale, with no royal umbrella and no music, and she knows something's wrong. He tells her everything, then gives instructions. Stay here. Serve my father and my mothers. Don't praise me in front of Bharata. Keep your vows, live simply, and wait for me. Valmiki says Sita answers out of love and anger together. Father, mother, brother, son: each lives out their own fortune. But a wife shares her husband's. If you've been sent to the forest, so have I. If you go today, I'll walk ahead of you, trampling the thorns and sharp grass so your path is easier. And she'd rather be in the forest with him, seeing the mountains and the lotus ponds, than in a palace without him. Rama decided for both of them, kindly and alone. Sita refuses to be decided for. Here's the teaching under her argument. You met the word at her wedding: a Hindu wife is a sahadharmachari, a companion on the path of dharma. At a Hindu wedding the couple takes seven steps together beside the sacred fire, and by the old words, at the seventh step they become friends. Sita is holding Rama to that. His duty is hers to share, thorns included. And that's still the promise when a couple takes those seven steps today: one road, walked together, even when it turns hard.
screen: `NO UMBRELLA, NO MUSIC.` · `RAMA'S PLAN: STAY HERE.` · `IF YOU'RE SENT TO THE FOREST, SO AM I.` · `SAHADHARMACHARI: A PARTNER IN DHARMA.` · then, large: `SEVEN STEPS, ONE ROAD.`

segments.voice: At a Hindu wedding the couple takes seven steps by the fire. Take seven slow breaths as seven steps. With each one, picture someone whose road you share: a partner, a parent, a friend. If you pray, offer each step to God for them; if you don't, simply wish them well. On the seventh, hold them as Sita held Rama: a friend whose road is yours too.
Sita's argument. Asked to stay behind, she answers with love and anger: a wife shares her husband's fortune, and if he's sent to the forest, so is she.
Hold on to it: a partner in dharma shares the road. Rama has one more try in him. Day five hundred twenty-six.

527.title: Sita changes Rama's mind
527.hook: Rama lists the forest's dangers, Sita answers every one, and he gives way; why devotees say Sita-Ram
527.carry: Sita-Ram: never one without the other
527.tomorrow: not everyone is calm. what will Lakshmana say?
527.howItsDone: Rama is rarely shown alone: temples and home shrines picture him with Sita, and devotees chant Sita-Ram and greet each other with Jai Siya Ram, her name first.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's argument began. If you're sent to the forest, so am I: a partner in dharma shares the road. Today Rama tries again, and so does she.
screen: `A PARTNER IN DHARMA SHARES THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: How do you stop someone you love from following you into danger, without forbidding it? Rama tries a list: every hardship the forest holds, one by one. It's love, mostly, and also a way of winning without saying no. He has watched his father break and his mother weep today, and he wants one person he loves kept safe. He means every word. And Sita, who has been patient, runs out of patience.
screen: `THE LIST OF DANGERS.` → `WINNING WITHOUT SAYING NO.` → `SITA LOSES HER PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: The forest is hard, Rama says. Lions roar from mountain caves. Rivers are full of crocodiles. You sleep on fallen leaves and eat whatever fruit you find, or nothing. Wind, darkness, hunger, snakes, thorns. Stay here. Sita answers his list item by item. With you, the grass will feel like a soft blanket; the fruit you bring me will taste like nectar. And when I was a girl, people who read the signs told my family I would one day live in a forest. Still Rama hesitates, and she stings. What was my father thinking, she asks, when he chose as his son-in-law a woman in the form of a man? Valmiki doesn't soften it. She's accusing Rama of failing at the one thing a protector is for: keeping her with him. Then she weeps. And Rama gives way. He holds her. I didn't know your mind, he says. I wouldn't want heaven itself without you. Come with me. In a story about a son obeying his father without a question, the wife questions, pushes, and changes her husband's mind. And this is why, in Hindu devotion, Rama is almost never alone. Temples and home shrines show Sita beside him. Devotees chant Sita-Ram, her name first, and many greet each other with Jai Siya Ram. Some traditions teach that you come to God through the Goddess at his side; that's a reading. The text says it plainer: he didn't want heaven without her.
screen: `LIONS, CROCODILES, THORNS.` · `A WOMAN IN THE FORM OF A MAN?` · `I DIDN'T KNOW YOUR MIND. COME.` · `SITA-RAM: HER NAME FIRST.` · then, large: `NEVER ONE WITHOUT THE OTHER.`

segments.voice: Try a practice many Hindus keep: japa, repeating a holy name. Breathe in, and silently say Sita; breathe out, and say Ram. Let the two names travel together, the way the two of them did. If you don't pray, breathe in on with, out on together, and think of someone you'd walk a hard road beside.
Sita's argument, won. She answers every danger, rebukes Rama sharply, and he relents: I didn't know your mind; come with me.
Hold on to it: Sita-Ram, never one without the other. Tomorrow, someone in the palace isn't calm at all. That's day five hundred twenty-seven.

528.title: Lakshmana's anger
528.hook: the loyal younger brother says out loud what everyone is thinking, and offers to fight the whole city
528.carry: dharma can pull two ways at once
528.tomorrow: fate or effort: will Lakshmana fight?
528.howItsDone: Hindu tradition remembers Lakshmana for a brother's devotion; in this outburst he argues from dharma, a protector's duty to the innocent, against Rama's dharma of keeping a father's word. 'Dharma is subtle' is the old phrase for such collisions. Where duties collide, the law books point to scripture, the conduct of good people, and one's own conscience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's argument, won, and Sita-Ram, never one without the other. Today we step back into Kausalya's room, where someone has been burning.

We've watched Rama be calm for days. Valmiki makes sure we know not everyone is. When Rama told his mother the news, Lakshmana stood silent in the room. Then, while Kausalya wept, he spoke, and out came the question the story has been holding back. This is wrong. Somebody should stop it. Why isn't anybody stopping it?
screen: `NOT EVERYONE IS CALM.` → `LAKSHMANA, SILENT IN THE ROOM.` → `WHY ISN'T ANYBODY STOPPING IT?`

segments.voice: Valmiki lets us hear every layer of Lakshmana's anger. First, fairness. Rama has done nothing wrong; who in the whole kingdom can name a single fault in him? To throw him out for no reason is against dharma itself. Second, the king. Lakshmana says what no one else will: the old man has been ruled by his desire for a young wife, and isn't fit to judge. He goes further still, with words against his own father that Valmiki records and we won't repeat here. Third, action. I'm armed, he tells Rama. I'm with you. If anyone in this city takes Bharata's side, I'll fight them all. Every word comes from love for his brother, and Hindu tradition remembers Lakshmana for that devotion. Kausalya, desperate, seizes on it. Listen to your brother, she tells Rama. Don't go. Now look at what just happened. Lakshmana isn't arguing against dharma. He's arguing from it. A prince's duty is to protect, and an innocent man is being thrown out. Rama will answer from dharma too: a son keeps his father's word. Both brothers are good, and dharma is pulling them in opposite directions. Hindu teachers have an old phrase for this: dharma is subtle. It isn't a rulebook you look things up in. Sometimes two real duties collide, and loyal people stand on both sides. So where do you look? The old Hindu law books name three places: scripture, the example of good people, and, in the end, your own conscience. That's still how many Hindu families weigh a hard choice. Tomorrow, what Rama does with his brother's argument.
screen: `RAMA HAS DONE NOTHING WRONG.` · `THE KING ISN'T FIT TO JUDGE.` · `I'M ARMED. I'M WITH YOU.` · `LISTEN TO YOUR BROTHER. DON'T GO.` · `PROTECT THE INNOCENT, OR KEEP THE WORD?` · then, large: `DHARMA CAN PULL TWO WAYS AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: Remember a time you were angry on someone else's behalf, and let a little of that heat come back. Notice where it lives: chest, hands, face. Then ask what duty it was defending: fairness, family, a friend. On each breath out, hold that duty gently next to the other one in the room, the one someone else was keeping. Picture a good person you trust standing between them: what would they see? If you pray, ask for the clarity to see both.
Lakshmana, Rama's loyal younger brother. Loyal to the bone, he says Rama has done no wrong and offers to fight the whole city for him.
Hold on to it: dharma can pull two ways at once. Lakshmana isn't finished. Until tomorrow.

529.title: Fate or effort
529.hook: only the weak blame fate, Lakshmana says, and then he has to decide what to do with his strength
529.carry: fate and effort, daiva and purushakara, both count
529.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often set Rama's speech on daiva, fate, beside Lakshmana's speech on purushakara, human effort, and leave listeners to weigh both.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana, loyal to the bone, arguing from dharma: dharma can pull two ways at once. Today, his argument, and his restraint.

A few days ago, Rama told Lakshmana not to blame Kaikeyi: what had happened was daiva, larger than any one person. It's a gentle idea, and Lakshmana hates it. He stands with his brow knotted, and Valmiki says he's breathing hard, like an angry snake in its hole. He answers with an argument people have quoted ever since, the other side of an old question: how much is fate, and how much is up to us?
screen: `DAIVA, RAMA SAID.` → `LAKSHMANA HATES IT.` → `HOW MUCH IS UP TO US?`

segments.voice: Here is Lakshmana's case. Fate is what weak people talk about. A real hero pushes fate aside with his own effort. Call this fate, and you've given up before you've tried. Then he holds up his arms. These aren't for decoration. They're for protecting you. Today the people will see which is stronger, fate or me. Let me take the kingdom for you. It's a powerful speech, and Valmiki doesn't make it foolish. In Hindu thought, effort, purushakara, is honored as seriously as fate, daiva. An old Sanskrit saying puts them together: a chariot doesn't move on one wheel. So Rama and Lakshmana are the tradition's two voices, and you can still hear both at a Hindu dinner table: a grandmother saying it was in your fate, a parent saying work harder. But watch Rama. He doesn't argue the philosophy again. He wipes away Lakshmana's tears and speaks to him as a brother. Know that I'm determined to keep our father's word. Stand with me in this. And Lakshmana listens, head lowered, still grieving, still angry, and silent. This is the restraint. He doesn't stop feeling the rage; he chooses not to spend it. He has the arms, the bow and the courage. What he gives his brother is the hardest effort a strong person can make: holding back. And at once the energy has somewhere to go. If you're going to the forest, Lakshmana says, then so am I.
screen: `ONLY THE WEAK TALK OF FATE.` · `THESE ARMS ARE FOR YOU.` · `ONE CHARIOT, TWO WHEELS: FATE AND EFFORT.` · `THE RAGE STAYS; HE DOESN'T SPEND IT.` · then, large: `THEN SO AM I.`

segments.voice: Close your hands into loose fists, and feel your own strength in them for a few breaths. Then slowly open them, palms up on your knees, and notice that the strength is still there. Breathe with them open; holding back isn't the same as being weak.
Purushakara, human effort, the old partner and rival of fate. Lakshmana argues that heroes push fate aside, then lowers his head, keeps his strength unspent, and chooses to go with Rama.
Hold on to it: fate and effort, daiva and purushakara, both count. And the strongest effort can be holding back. Day five hundred twenty-nine, done.

530.hook: Lakshmana asks to go, and the text is silent about the wife he leaves behind
530.tomorrow: why does Rama give everything away?

segments.voice: Yesterday: purushakara, human effort, with fate beside it. Lakshmana argued, then lowered his head and held back. Today, his anger becomes a job.
screen: `THE RAGE STAYS; HE DOESN'T SPEND IT.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana was in the room while Sita won her argument. He heard her say she'd walk ahead of Rama through the thorns. Now he has his own case to make, and it sounds like a sibling who turns up on moving day unasked and heads straight for the heaviest boxes. It isn't eloquent. It's practical: who carries what, who walks where, who finds the food. And it ends with a job.
screen: `HE HEARD SITA WIN.` → `CARRYING THE HEAVY BOXES.` → `PRACTICAL, NOT ELOQUENT.`

segments.voice: Lakshmana falls at Rama's feet, tears in his eyes, and asks to go. Rama says no at first, with a good reason. Someone must look after our mothers, Kausalya and Sumitra. The king is consumed by Kaikeyi now. Lakshmana has an answer. Bharata will honor them, and if he doesn't, I'll deal with him. Kausalya has wealth enough to support a thousand like me. Then the practical part. I'll walk ahead of you with my bow, carrying a spade and a basket. I'll find the path, gather fruit and roots, and do the work, while you and Sita enjoy the mountains. Rama is moved, and says yes. Then he gives Lakshmana a job: bring the divine bows and armor the god Varuna gave us, kept at our teacher's house. So the rage that wanted to fight the city becomes a younger brother carrying weapons, a spade and a basket. Not anger erased, but anger given work. Hindus have a word for this: seva, service offered as devotion. Lakshmana is remembered as its picture, the brother who walks ahead with the tools. It's why someone washing pots in a temple kitchen, or serving a festival meal, calls it seva, not chores. And here's what the text doesn't say. Lakshmana is married. The day Rama married Sita, he married Sita's sister Urmila. Valmiki doesn't tell us what Lakshmana said to her, or whether she asked to come. Later poets noticed that silence, and some filled it. Valmiki leaves the space empty.
screen: `WHO WILL CARE FOR OUR MOTHERS?` · `A BOW, A SPADE AND A BASKET.` · `ANGER GIVEN WORK.` · `SEVA: SERVICE AS DEVOTION.` · then, large: `AND URMILA? THE TEXT IS SILENT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone whose seva in your life went mostly unspoken: someone who stayed behind, covered for you, kept things running. On each breath in, remember something specific they did. On each breath out, send them thanks, even silently. Then choose one small act of seva for tomorrow, done for someone without needing it noticed.
Urmila, Lakshmana's wife, Sita's sister, married the same day, left in a silence Valmiki never fills. The anger that wanted to fight becomes a brother walking ahead with a bow, a spade and a basket.
Hold on to it: seva, anger turned into service. And somewhere in the palace, Urmila stays. See you tomorrow.

531.title: Rama gives it all away
531.hook: before he leaves, Rama gives everything away, and makes a poor old man throw his stick
531.carry: dana: give generously, and give humbly
531.howItsDone: Hindus give dana, gifts, at turning points such as weddings, festivals and journeys; the Taittiriya Upanishad asks that it be given with faith and with modesty, and Rama's apology to Trijata shows the modest part.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Urmila, left in Valmiki's silence, and seva, Lakshmana's anger turned into service. Today the departure begins, with giving.

Armlets. Earrings. A golden girdle. A herd of cows. On the day Rama leaves, his rooms empty out, piece by piece, into other people's hands. Leaving a home can come with a day like this, sad and oddly freeing at once: the couch to a cousin, the plants to whoever will water them. Here it's a prince's wealth. And in the middle of it, Valmiki tells a small story with a joke in it, on a day built for tears.
screen: `ARMLETS, EARRINGS, COWS.` → `A PRINCE'S WEALTH, GIVEN AWAY.` → `A JOKE ON A DAY OF TEARS.`

segments.voice: Rama sends for Suyajna, the son of his teacher Vasishtha, and gives him armlets, earrings and jewels. Sita sends a necklace and a golden girdle to Suyajna's wife. Gifts go to teachers, to old household servants, to everyone who depends on Rama for a living, so no one is left without support while he's gone. Then the story. Near Ayodhya lives a very poor brahmin named Trijata, old and thin, who scrapes a living digging in the fields. His wife hears Rama is giving things away. Go, she says. So Trijata stands before the prince, and Rama, of all things, teases him. I haven't yet given away even a thousand of my cows. Throw your staff. However far it lands, every cow up to that point is yours. The old man ties up his clothes and throws with every bit of strength he has. The staff flies across the river Sarayu into a pasture full of cattle. Rama embraces him and gives him every cow up to that spot. Then he apologizes. Don't be offended. It was a joke. I only wanted to see the strength in you. This is dana, giving, one of the oldest duties in Hinduism, and Hindus still give it at turning points: weddings, festivals, journeys. An Upanishad teacher sends his students home with a short list on how: give with faith, give with modesty, give with understanding. Rama gives a fortune, then says sorry to the poorest man in line. That's the modest part, and the hardest. Grief hasn't made him small, and wealth hasn't made him proud.
screen: `GIFTS SO NO ONE IS LEFT WITHOUT.` · `THROW YOUR STAFF.` · `IT WAS A JOKE. FORGIVE ME.` · `DANA: WITH FAITH, WITH MODESTY.` · then, large: `GRIEF HASN'T MADE HIM SMALL.`

segments.voice: Look around in your mind at what you own, and pick one thing someone else would use. Picture handing it over the way the Upanishad asks: with faith, with modesty, without needing thanks. If you pray, offer it to God first; if you don't, simply wish the receiver well. Then rest in the breath, lighter by one thing.
The departure, part one: giving. Rama and Sita give their wealth away, and Rama gives poor Trijata every cow up to where his staff lands, then says sorry for the joke.
Hold on to it: dana, give generously, and give humbly. That's day five hundred thirty-one.

532.title: Sumitra's blessing
532.hook: bark clothes are brought out, Sita doesn't know how to put them on, and Lakshmana's mother gives him one verse
532.tomorrow: why does Rama slip away before dawn?
532.howItsDone: Sumitra's verse, rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi, is taught as a picture of how love makes any place home; Tulsidas's Hindi Ramcharitmanas gives her a line in the same spirit: Ayodhya is wherever Rama lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the departure began with dana, giving, and an old man's staff flying across the river. Today, the goodbyes, and the end of a week.

Rama, Sita and Lakshmana walk to the palace on foot. Crowds line the streets, and Valmiki lets us hear them: people who cheered for the coronation this morning are weeping now, and some openly criticize the king. Inside, the whole family is waiting: the old king, the queens, counselors, priests. This is the last room before the road. And someone has brought a pile of clothes made of tree bark.
screen: `THEY WALK TO THE PALACE.` → `THE CROWDS WEEP.` → `A PILE OF BARK CLOTHES.`

segments.voice: Dasharatha begs Rama, one last time, to stay just one night. Rama gently refuses. The king orders the army and the treasury to go with him, and Rama turns it down. Why keep the rope, he asks, once you've given away the elephant? Then Kaikeyi hands out the bark garments. Rama and Lakshmana trade their fine clothes for them. Sita stands holding hers, confused. She has never worn anything like it. She tries, can't, and starts to cry. Rama ties it for her, over her silk. Vasishtha, watching, finally loses his temper with Kaikeyi. Sita was never part of the boons, he says. Then the mothers speak. And Sumitra gives her son Lakshmana one verse: rāmaṃ daśarathaṃ viddhi māṃ viddhi janakātmajām, ayodhyām aṭavīṃ viddhi, gaccha tāta yathāsukham. Think of Rama as your father Dasharatha. Think of Sita as me, your mother. Think of the forest as Ayodhya. Go, my son, and go happily. A mother sends her son into exile by telling him he isn't leaving home at all. Centuries later, Tulsidas, retelling the Ramayana in Hindi, gives Sumitra a line in the same spirit: Ayodhya is wherever Rama lives. For devotees, that's the teaching under the verse. Home isn't a city. It's being near God and the people you love. It's why a family that moves across an ocean can carry its little home shrine with it, and still be home.
screen: `SITA CAN'T TIE THE BARK.` · `VASISHTHA: SITA WASN'T IN THE BOONS.` · `SUMITRA: THE FOREST IS AYODHYA.` · `AYODHYA IS WHEREVER RAMA LIVES.` · then, large: `RĀMAṂ DAŚARATHAṂ VIDDHI.`

segments.voice: Try Sumitra's words on wherever you are. If you pray, picture the face of God you know best, here in this room with you; if you don't, picture the people you love. On a breath in, notice this room, this chair, this light; on a breath out, let it be home. If your mind drifts somewhere you'd rather be, gently bring it back, and call this Ayodhya.
The departure, part two: the goodbyes. Bark clothes, Rama tying Sita's, and Sumitra's verse: think of the forest as Ayodhya.
Hold on to it: Ayodhya is wherever Rama is. Next week, the road. Day five hundred thirty-two, done.
